senses: Extremely fun.
examples: I figured I'd never be able to compete with what I considered the most perfect wedding in existence, so I concentrated on making mine superfun.
Thanks to Sherry Yard, for making Spago a superfun place to work from when in So Cal.
Where, according to the rusty sign dangling over the entrance, a superfun, amazing time awaits the entire family.

senses: One who signs their name (applies their signature to something).
One who signs up another.
examples: Near-synonyms: undersigned, subscriber
John Hancock is a famous signer of the Declaration of Independence.
The most prolific signers were to be amply rewarded by the sales-bonus structure.

senses: One who uses a flag or signal, for example to direct traffic or to start a race.
panties (short underpants for women or girls); underpants
ety: Borrowed from Japanese パンツ (pantsu), from English pants.

senses: Having two modes or forms.
A Philippine dish in which pork or chicken is slowly cooked in a sauce including soy sauce, vinegar, and crushed garlic.
ety: From Spanish adobo, from Old French adober (“equip a horseman”) (perhaps via Catalan), from the same Germanic root as dab, dub. Compare French daube (earlier dobe (1571), adobbe (1598)), Italian dobba (1549), adobbo (1570).

senses: A body of water impounded within an enclosure, such as a reservoir.
The act of impounding.
Within or near a coast
The virtue of "practical wisdom" as posited by Aristotle.
ety: From Ancient Greek φρόνησις (phrónēsis, “practical wisdom”), from φρονέω (phronéō, “to think”), from φρήν (phrḗn, “mind”).

senses: A slight or surface burn.
A discolouration caused by heat.
ety: From Middle English scorchen, scorcnen (“to make dry; parch”), perhaps an alteration of earlier *scorpnen, from Old Norse skorpna (“to shrivel up”).

senses: A Japanese flute which is tuned to a pentatonic scale and is end-blown like a recorder instead of being held transversely like the Western transverse flute.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 尺八 (しゃくはち, shakuhachi), from 尺 (tsyhek, an archaic measure of length approximately equal to 30 centimeters) + 八 (peat, “eight”), corresponding to the standard length of the instrument (approximately 55 centimeters).

senses: Synonym of dandy or hammock litter, a strong cloth suspended from a pole or set of poles used as an open sedan chair.
Synonym of litter, used in religious processions of saints' figurines.
ety: From Portuguese andor, from Malayalam, from Sanskrit हिन्दोल (hindola, “swinging cradle, hammock litter, dooly”). Compare dooly from Sanskrit दुल् (dul) via Hindi.

senses: A type of rough jacket with a hood.
Through or across an epithelium.
Synonym of mucoid.
To engage in ageplay; to role-play as a different age than one’s actual chronological age.
Having a crotch or fork; forked.
Stone that is quarried in thin pieces.
A kind of nougat made with almonds, honey, and a light mousse of egg whites.
examples: The dark montelimars that are common are made by adding cocoa powder, usually to a less aerated confection.

senses: The set of frames that constitute the layout of a webpage.
examples: The reloading of the frameset is obviously less attractive than simply changing the location of one frame.

senses: Total color blindness; the total inability to distinguish colors due to the absence of cone cells in the eyes.
ety: From German Achromatopsie, from Ancient Greek ἀχρώματος (akhrṓmatos), from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”), + -opsie. By surface analysis, a- + chromato- + -opsia.

senses: The movable swing frame of a loom, carrying the reed for separating the warp threads and beating up the weft.
ety: From Middle English lathe (“turning-lathe; stand”), from Old Norse hlað (“pile, heap”)—compare dialectal Danish lad (“stand, support frame”) (as in drejelad (“turning-lathe”), savelad (“saw bench”)), dialectal Norwegian la, lad (“pile, small wall”), dialectal Swedish lad (“folding table, lay of a loom”)—from hlaða (“to load”). More at lade.

senses: impetuosity, prowess, vigour
ety: From Old French derroi, desroi, desrei, from des- (from Latin dis-) + roi, rei, rai (“order”). See array and disarray.

senses: One who believes in functionalism.
A garnish of vegetables cut into long, thin strips.
ety: From French julienne (1722), from given name Jules or Julien, presumably from an otherwise unknown chef of that name. Originally used in potage julienne (“Julienne potage, soup in the manner of Jules/Julien”), meaning “soup made from thin slices”; this sense is now known as chiffonade.

senses: A transistor radio.
examples: He spent most of his time in his darkened storeroom with a tranny and an earplug while his kid ran riot in the classroom.
We talk, and I listen to Radio Luxembourg on my tranny – I have a little earplug, so if any teachers come in they won't hear it.

senses: A mariposa lily (Calochortus spp.).
Aluminium foil.
Transmasculine.
examples: Quinn Eades is a queer transmasc writer and poet. Jamie & Quinn are in love. The images and poetry are from their forthcoming book, Queerdom.

senses: To drool saliva from the mouth; to slobber.
To be drooled out of someone’s mouth.
To smear with saliva issuing from the mouth.
To be besmeared with saliva.
ety: From Middle English slaveren, from Old Norse slafra (“to slaver”), probably imitative. Doublet of slabber.

senses: The craft of making stringed musical instruments.
ety: From French lutherie (“manufacture of stringed instruments”). Doublet of luthiery.

senses: To work from home, sometimes for part of a working day or week, using a computer connected to one's employer's network or via the Internet.
A ballet move involving a beating action with an extended leg
examples: Ernst and Watson are superb dancers--extraordinarily agile and acrobatic, and their unison spins, battements, and body lines showed a split-second timing.

senses: An SI unit of time equal to 10⁻¹⁸ seconds. Symbol: as
examples: I can think at the speed of light, I can perceive events that last for less than an attosecond, I can run faster than time. What do I see when I run across the country, Superman? I see everything. And everyone.
The observation and manipulation of electron dynamics in matter call for attosecond light pulses, routinely available from high-order harmonic generation driven by few-femtosecond lasers.

senses: A classical convex moulding carved with an egg and dart ornament.
ety: From Italian ovolo, from Latin ōvum (“egg”). Doublet of ovule.
examples: Decoration inside: six linked palmettes with 9 petals around a band of ovolos between incised lines, surrounded by 13 palmettes linked around a band of ovolos.
Using a template or a good eye to guide the paring chisel, slice off the corners of the tenon ovolos at 45 degrees.

senses: To subject to bitter verbal abuse.
To vitriolize.
ety: From Middle English vitriol, from Old French vitriol, from Medieval Latin vitriolum (“sulfuric acid”), from vitrum (“glass”).

senses: An instrument or contrivance to size articles, or to determine their size by a standard, or to separate and distribute them according to size.
An instrument or tool for bringing anything to an exact size.
An object used at the airport to test to see if a carry on or personal item is the correct size allowed by the airline.
The area of the forest cleared of trees.
examples: Can clearcuts increase bird species richness in managed forests?

senses: The science of dating samples of rock or sediment.
Any one of the methods by which the age of different samples of rock can be determined.
The division of ancient time into named subdivisions / periods
examples: Geochronology allows us to see more precisely how the world has evolved.
The history of the East–Antarctic shield has been uncovered through uranium–lead geochronology.

senses: The process or instance of ovipositing, laying eggs.
ety: From ovi- (“egg”) + Latin positiō (“the action of placing”).
examples: If an opsiblastic egg is produced by an individual, it is usually the last oviposition by that animal even if it is also the first.
